Lecture 1 · The definition of a group

0 Which property says that multiplying two elements of G produces another element of G?

Here is the hint — try once more. The operation must close on the underlying set. Closure means that the group product is a map G × G → G.

Lecture 1 · Examples

0 How many elements does the symmetry group D₃ of an equilateral triangle have?

Count the rotations and the reflections separately.

Here is the hint — try once more. D₃ contains three rotations and three reflections, hence six elements.

Lecture 1 · The definition of a group

0 What does rs ≠ sr demonstrate about D₃?

Here is the hint — try once more. An abelian group has the same product in either order. The unequal products exhibit non-commutativity, so D₃ is non-abelian.

Lecture 1 · Cosets and Lagrange’s theorem

0 Which number cannot be the order of a subgroup of a group of order 12?

Here is the hint — try once more. Use divisibility, not only inequality. Lagrange's theorem requires a subgroup order to divide 12; 5 does not.

Lecture 1 · Cosets and Lagrange’s theorem

0 What follows for every group of prime order?

Here is the hint — try once more. Apply Lagrange's theorem to a non-identity element. A non-identity element must have order equal to the prime, so it generates the group.

Lecture 2 · Conjugacy

0 For transformations of space, (hgh−1)(x′)=h(g(x))(hgh^{-1})(x')=h(g(x))(hgh−1)(x′)=h(g(x)) where x′=h(x)x'=h(x)x′=h(x). What does hgh−1hgh^{-1}hgh−1 therefore do?

Lecture 2 · Simple groups and composition series [self-study]

0 Which abelian groups are simple?

Here is the hint — try once more. In an abelian group every subgroup is normal. What can a simple abelian group therefore have no room for? Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, so a simple abelian group can have no proper nontrivial subgroup at all — which forces cyclic of prime order. C4C_4C4​ is cyclic and not simple, since ⟨g2⟩\langle g^2\rangle⟨g2⟩ sits inside it. The answer “none” has the right premise and the wrong conclusion: CpC_pCp​ has no subgroup left to be normal.

Lecture 2 · Simple groups and composition series [self-study]

0 C4C_4C4​ and the Klein four-group both have composition factors C2,C2C_2,C_2C2​,C2​. What does that show?

Here is the hint — try once more. Jordan–Hölder compares two series of ONE group. Does it say anything about two different groups? Jordan–Hölder says any two composition series of the same group agree, and that is all it says. Building a group back up from given factors — the extension problem — has many inequivalent solutions, so the atoms do not determine the molecule: C4C_4C4​ has an element of order 444 and the Klein four-group has none.

Lecture 4 · Maschke’s theorem: complete reducibility

Lecture 4 · Unitarity: the averaging trick

0 The proof that a finite group's representation can be made unitary rewrites ∑h∈G⟨ρ(hg)u,ρ(hg)v⟩0\sum_{h\in G}\inner{\rho(hg)u}{\rho(hg)v}_0∑h∈G​⟨ρ(hg)u,ρ(hg)v⟩0​ as ∑h′∈G⟨ρ(h′)u,ρ(h′)v⟩0\sum_{h'\in G}\inner{\rho(h')u}{\rho(h')v}_0∑h′∈G​⟨ρ(h′)u,ρ(h′)v⟩0​. What makes that step valid?

Here is the hint — try once more. As hhh runs once through GGG, what does hghghg do? Right multiplication by ggg is a bijection of GGG: that is cancellation, the Latin-square property of the Cayley table. So the second sum has the same terms in a different order, and nothing about ρ\rhoρ is used. Unitarity for ⟨⋅,⋅⟩0\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_0⟨⋅,⋅⟩0​ is false in general, and it is what the theorem proves for the averaged product, not something it may assume for the old one. Re-indexing a sum over the group is the averaging trick, and it returns in the orthogonality relations and the projection formulae.

Lecture 4 · Maschke’s theorem: complete reducibility

Lecture 4 · Schur’s lemma

0 Let VVV be irreducible, WWW any representation, and T∈Hom⁡G(V,W)T\in\Hom_G(V,W)T∈HomG​(V,W) nonzero. What follows without knowing anything more about WWW?

Lecture 4 · Schur’s lemma

0 A Hamiltonian HHH commutes with every ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g), and an irreducible representation of dimension 333 occurs exactly once in the state space. How many distinct eigenvalues can HHH have on that three-dimensional subspace?

Because the representation occurs only once, HHH maps that subspace to itself. What must an operator be that commutes with an irreducible action?

Here is the hint — try once more. One. On a multiplicity-one irreducible, HHH is an intertwiner of the representation with itself, so Schur's lemma makes it E id⁡E\,\idEid: a single energy, threefold degenerate. When the irreducible occurs mmm times, HHH may mix the mmm copies, and its eigenvalues then come in threefold multiplets.

Lecture 5 · The regular representation

Lecture 5 · The regular representation

Lecture 5 · Character tables

Lecture 6 · The block-diagonalisation theorem

Lecture 6 · The block-diagonalisation theorem

0 For a nonlinear classical system, a finite symmetry group only maps solutions to solutions. Why do quantum mechanics, and the small vibrations of Lecture 7, get far more out of it?

Here is the hint — try once more. What does the superposition principle make of the set of states? Linearity: superposition makes the states (or the small displacements) a vector space and the symmetry a linear representation on it. Then every energy level, or normal-mode frequency, is a representation, and its dimension is constrained by the irreducible ones. Noether's theorem needs a continuous family of symmetries, and a finite group stays finite.

Lecture 7 · Symmetry block-diagonalises DDD

0 Projecting ammonia's internal coordinates gives the symmetric stretch, the umbrella and two EEE pairs (asymmetric stretch and asymmetric bend). Which of them are normal modes by symmetry alone?

Here is the hint — try once more. By the block theorem, DDD acts on the isotypic component of type iii through an mi×mim_i\times m_imi​×mi​ matrix F(i)F^{(i)}F(i). When does that leave no choice? The normal modes are their eigenvectors: generically two combinations of the symmetric stretch and the umbrella, and likewise two combinations of the EEE pairs, with one 2×22\times22×2 matrix for both partners. A projected vector is a normal mode by symmetry alone only when its type occurs once, as water's B1B_1B1​ stretch does. Being fully symmetric, or degenerate, does not help: the umbrella and the symmetric stretch are both A1A_1A1​, which is exactly why they mix. Lecture 8 · Selection rules and the Wigner–Eckart theorem

0 An operator family TαT_\alphaTα​ transforms as VTV_TVT​. What does Theorem 8.8 say about when it can connect a level of type V(i)V^{(i)}V(i) to a level of type V(f)V^{(f)}V(f)?

Here is the hint — try once more. The theorem proves that something must vanish. Can an argument of that kind show that something does not vanish? If V(f)V^{(f)}V(f) is absent from VT⊗V(i)V_T\otimes V^{(i)}VT​⊗V(i), every amplitude ⟨fμ∣Tα∣iν⟩\bra{f_\mu}T_\alpha\ket{i_\nu}⟨fμ​∣Tα​∣iν​⟩ vanishes. The converse fails: symmetry can forbid a transition but never guarantee one, nor say how strong an allowed line is, so "if and only if" claims too much. The wavefunction is exp⁡(−qTD1/2q/2ℏ)\exp\bigl(-q^{\mathsf T}D^{1/2}q/2\hbar\bigr)exp(−qTD1/2q/2ℏ), and replacing qqq by ρ(g)−1q\rho(g)^{-1}qρ(g)−1q leaves qTD1/2qq^{\mathsf T}D^{1/2}qqTD1/2q unchanged, because ρ(g)TD1/2ρ(g)=D1/2\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}D^{1/2}\rho(g)=D^{1/2}ρ(g)TD1/2ρ(g)=D1/2 when ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) is orthogonal and commutes with DDD. Lecture 8 · Level splitting under symmetry reduction

0 Restricted to CsC_sCs​, a C3vC_{3v}C3v​ doublet EEE becomes A′⊕A′′A'\oplus A''A′⊕A′′. Why does Section 8.4 say that the level splits only generically?

Here is the hint — try once more. Must A′A'A′ and A′′A''A′′ share an energy? Must they differ? A′A'A′ and A′′A''A′′ are inequivalent, so no symmetry ties their energies together: each type has its own block. But nothing forces the two numbers apart either, and for a special perturbation they can coincide, an accidental degeneracy as in Lecture 6. "Generically" means for every perturbation with CsC_sCs​ symmetry except such accidents.

Lecture 8 · Level splitting under symmetry reduction

0 Doubling one hydrogen's mass is not a small perturbation. What of the restriction C3v→CsC_{3v}\to C_sC3v​→Cs​ still holds for NH2D\mathrm{NH_2D}NH2​D, and what is lost?

Here is the hint — try once more. Which step needs the perturbation to be small: restricting the representation, or the perturbation theory? Restriction of the whole vibration space stays exact, since NH2D\mathrm{NH_2D}NH2​D has exact CsC_sCs​ symmetry: its vibrations carry Γvib↓Cs=4A′⊕2A′′\Gamma_{\mathrm{vib}}{\downarrow}C_s=4A'\oplus2A''Γvib​↓Cs​=4A′⊕2A′′, and so generically six distinct fundamentals. Smallness is needed only to follow an isolated parent level and keep its descendants nearby, and that fails here: the 1627 cm−11627\ \mathrm{cm}^{-1}1627 cm−1 bend of NH3\mathrm{NH_3}NH3​ gives lines near 160016001600 and 1390 cm−11390\ \mathrm{cm}^{-1}1390 cm−1. A merger would be an accident, which "generically" excludes.

Lecture 8 · Selection rules and the Wigner–Eckart theorem

0 In a perfect octahedral complex, why is the d→dd\to dd→d absorption across the gap Δ\DeltaΔ forbidden, and why is it seen at all?

Here is the hint — try once more. Use the parity labels of Oh=O×{E,i}O_h=O\times\{E,i\}Oh​=O×{E,i}. Is VT⊗V(i)V_T\otimes V^{(i)}VT​⊗V(i) even or odd? The ddd levels are even (ege_geg​, t2gt_{2g}t2g​) and the dipole is odd, so VT⊗V(i)V_T\otimes V^{(i)}VT​⊗V(i) is odd and contains no even V(f)V^{(f)}V(f): every amplitude vanishes. The mechanism the notes give for the line is that vibrations break the inversion for a moment, which is why such colours are pale. Different dimensions forbid nothing, and the A1A_1A1​ argument asks the wrong question: the rule asks for V(f)V^{(f)}V(f) in VT⊗V(i)V_T\otimes V^{(i)}VT​⊗V(i).
